subject: physics_2
question_text: Explain the terms 'chain reaction' and 'multiplication factor'. How a chain reaction is sustained?

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. PRINTED ERROR CORRECTED. The book (p.51) writes "If they again participate in FUSION reaction nine neutrons are produced". The process that turns three neutrons into nine is FISSION: fusion joins light nuclei and releases no neutron chain. The numbers 3, 9, 27 in the book are the fission generations, so only the word is wrong. Hand-checked: 3, 3² = 9, 3³ = 27 is a geometric progression of ratio 3, matching the book's "geometric progression". The real average is about 2.5 neutrons per fission of ²³⁵U; the book rounds to three.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: How the neutron numbers grow
steps.mark_note: Three neutrons per fission, then 9, then 27
lines: In nuclear fission, nearly three neutrons are
produced when one uranium nucleus is split.
If these again take part in FISSION, nine
neutrons are produced; in the next generation
the number becomes 27.
The neutron number grows in geometric
progression, so the whole uranium is used up
in a few seconds.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The sequence 3, 9, 27 and the words geometric progression.
steps.why: The book prints "if they again participate in fusion reaction nine neutrons are produced". That must read FISSION: fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen and produces no neutron chain, while the numbers 3, 9, 27 are exactly the fission generations.
common_mistakes: Copying the book and writing "fusion". Every generation here is a fission.
Saying the growth is in arithmetic progression. Each generation multiplies by three.

recall.must_convey: That one fission gives about three neutrons, which cause further fissions giving nine and then 27 neutrons, a geometric progression.
accept: three then nine then twenty seven neutrons
each fission gives about three neutrons
reject: self sustained fission reaction is called chain reaction

steps.memory_tip: Three, nine, twenty-seven: powers of three, one per generation.

steps.label: Chain reaction defined
lines: This type of self-sustained fission reaction is
called a chain reaction.
It releases a large amount of energy, because
each fission releases about 200 MeV.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The phrase "self-sustained fission reaction".
steps.why: The reaction sustains itself because the particle it needs to start — a neutron — is also a product of it.
common_mistakes: Defining a chain reaction without the word fission.

recall.must_convey: That a self-sustained fission reaction of this kind, releasing a large amount of energy, is called a chain reaction.
accept: releases a large amount of energy
reject: ratio of neutrons in the present generation

steps.memory_tip: Fission needs a neutron and makes neutrons — the reaction is self-sustained.

steps.label: Multiplication factor K
steps.mark_note: Ratio of neutrons in successive generations
lines: Neutron multiplication factor (K): the ratio of
the number of neutrons in the present
generation to the number in the previous
generation.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The ratio between two successive generations.
steps.why: K compares one generation with the one before it, so it says at once whether the reaction is growing, steady or dying without counting any absolute number of neutrons.
common_mistakes: Defining K as the number of neutrons per fission. It is a ratio between generations.
Giving K a unit. It is a pure number.

recall.must_convey: That the neutron multiplication factor K is the ratio of the number of neutrons in the present generation to the number in the previous generation.
accept: ratio of neutrons in present generation to previous generation

steps.memory_tip: K is this generation divided by the previous generation.

steps.label: How it is sustained
steps.mark_note: K = 1 steady, K > 1 growing, K < 1 stops
lines: A chain reaction is sustained when K ≥ 1.
K = 1: the reaction is steady and controlled,
as in a nuclear reactor.
K > 1: the reaction grows rapidly and is
uncontrolled, as in an atom bomb.
K < 1: the reaction dies away.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. All three cases, with K = 1 named as the reactor.
steps.why: K = 1 is the boundary between a reaction that fades and one that runs away, which is why a reactor is designed to be held exactly at it.
common_mistakes: Saying a reactor runs at K > 1. That is the bomb condition.
Giving only the K = 1 case. The question asks how the reaction is sustained.

recall.must_convey: That a chain reaction is sustained when K is at least 1: K = 1 gives a steady controlled reaction as in a reactor, K greater than 1 gives an uncontrolled growing reaction, and K less than 1 stops.
accept: K greater than or equal to one
K less than one the reaction dies away
reject: ratio of neutrons in two generations

steps.memory_tip: Below 1 it fades, at 1 it holds, above 1 it grows fast.

insider_note: Write the generation numbers 3, 9, 27 — they show the geometric growth the examiner is looking for. The printed book says "fusion" here; it is fission.
